title: A City Starved and Broken
overview: This poem mourns Jerusalem's fall to Babylon around 587 BC, dwelling on the long famine of the siege, the people it blames, and a final word about the end of punishment.

parts.label: Gold gone dull (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The tarnished gold and scattered stones may be the temple's real gold and building stones, thrown into the streets when it burned, or a picture of the city's people. Either way, the people of Zion (another name for Jerusalem), once treated as precious, are now handled like cheap clay pots.

parts.label: Children with nothing (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Even wild animals nurse their young, but starving mothers had no milk, so they seemed as uncaring as the ostrich, which people then believed abandoned its eggs. Wealthy families raised on fine food and costly dyed cloth now lie on rubbish heaps.

parts.label: A slow death by hunger (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Sodom, a city remembered for its sudden destruction, fell in a moment, while Jerusalem starved for months under siege until even its healthy, handsome leaders were unrecognizable. The poem says plainly that some mothers ate their own children, a horror the law of Moses had warned could happen in a siege.

parts.label: Who the poet blames (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: The poet sees the fire as the LORD's anger, so shocking that the kings and peoples of the earth had not believed enemies could ever enter Jerusalem's gates. It blames prophets and priests who shed innocent blood; they now wander as outcasts, shunned with the cry "Unclean!" that the law of Moses required people with certain skin diseases to call out.

parts.label: Help that never came (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: The people watched for an ally, most likely Egypt, that never rescued them, and the Babylonians hunted down those who fled. "The LORD's anointed" is the king, probably Zedekiah, who was captured while trying to escape after the people had believed their lives depended on him.

parts.label: A word to Edom (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: Edom, a neighboring nation related to Israel, seems to have celebrated Jerusalem's fall, so the poet bitterly tells it to enjoy this while it can, because the "cup" of God's anger will reach Edom too. The last word for Jerusalem is quieter: its punishment is ending and its exile will not be prolonged.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the poem's claim that the LORD poured out this disaster in anger should be read as a direct statement of how God acts, or as a grieving people's honest attempt to make sense of catastrophe that the Bible preserves without fully endorsing.
think: When a disaster strikes, why do people so often search for someone or something to blame, and does finding a cause make grief easier or harder to carry?
